title: Ukraine’s Cardboard Maidan Shows That the People Still Matter
gist: A week of street protests in Kyiv forced Volodymyr Zelensky to partially reverse the July 15 firing of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and to dismiss army chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, showing that under martial law with elections suspended, protest is Ukraine's only functioning check on executive power. The fight is substantively about whether Ukraine rebuilds its army around drones and competitive procurement or keeps a manpower-attrition, discretionary-contract model.

themes.theme: Street pressure as Ukraine's only working check

insights.claim: Mass protests in Kyiv forced Volodymyr Zelensky to reverse a defense-leadership decision within one week — he fired Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov on July 15 and reversed course seven days later after nightly crowds gathered outside the presidential office.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Ukrainian wartime policy is now reversible by street pressure on a one-week timescale; personnel and procurement decisions carry political-reversal risk for anyone contracting with Kyiv.
insights.locator: It took the crowds outside Ukrainian President

insights.claim: With elections suspended under martial law, protest is the only functioning constraint on Ukrainian executive power, and Zelensky has now bowed to street demands twice since 2022 — the anti-corruption agency law in July 2025 and the Fedorov dismissal in July 2026.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Model Ukrainian institutional risk through the street, not the ballot box: watch Kyiv crowd size as the leading indicator of policy U-turns.
insights.quote: The streets have learned that Zelensky listens, and even under martial law, with elections suspended, protests remain the one check on power that works.
insights.locator: This is the second time since the full-scale invasion

insights.claim: Ukrainian officials badly misread the protest's staying power, with one senior official predicting the demonstrations needed only a 'couple of days to die' before they instead grew and expanded their demands.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Government-sourced reassurance about protest durability has proven unreliable in Kyiv; discount official guidance on political stability.
insights.locator: The initial response inside the government

insights.claim: Protest organizers refused to demobilize after Syrskyi's dismissal, saying demonstrations will continue until Fedorov is restored to the Defense Ministry rather than given one of the vague alternative posts Zelensky has offered.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: The partial concession has not cleared the political overhang; further Kyiv instability is the base case in the near term.
insights.locator: But even though Zelensky has accepted the fact

insights.claim: Zelensky dismissed commander in chief Oleksandr Syrskyi and appointed Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi — a combat commander associated with the 2014 Mariupol armored breakthrough, the defense of Kryvyi Rih and the liberation of Kherson's western bank — as new army chief.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: A generational handover in Ukrainian high command raises the odds of doctrine shifting toward maneuver and technology rather than static attrition defense.
insights.locator: Zelensky heard them out, at least in part.

insights.claim: The same July shakeup removed Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko and installed Serhiy Koretsky, a former chief of state gas company Naftogaz, as her replacement.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: A Naftogaz alumnus running the government signals energy-sector priority in Ukrainian economic policy and reconstruction contracting.
insights.locator: Zelensky thought otherwise. He dismissed Fedorov

insights.claim: Fedorov's dismissal triggered immediate resignations across the defense-tech network: Col. Pavlo Yelizarov quit as deputy commander of the air force, along with drone fundraiser Serhii Sternenko and military technology expert Serhii Beskrestnov.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Ukraine's drone-innovation network is personnel-dependent and can be disrupted by a single ministerial change — relevant to any defense-tech supply chain routed through Kyiv.
insights.locator: The fallout was immediate.

insights.claim: Fedorov played a key role, alongside other senior officials, in pressuring Zelensky to remove Andriy Yermak as head of the Office of the President; Yermak resigned in November 2025 under a combination of internal counsel and mounting foreign pressure.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Shows foreign pressure plus internal coalitions can shift Ukraine's inner circle — a lever Western creditors and donors have already used successfully.
insights.locator: Fedorov also brought enemies.

insights.claim: Fedorov's military plan was to rebuild Ukraine's army around technology rather than manpower, with a drone line strong enough that Ukraine could stand as a fortress and curtail Russian advances with or without a signed peace deal.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: The 'fortress by drone line' concept is the core demand-driver for European and Ukrainian UAV production regardless of ceasefire outcomes.
insights.locator: The second front for Fedorov was the high military command.

insights.claim: A senior Ukrainian government official credited Fedorov with exactly two big achievements — disabling Starlink for Russian forces and heavily expanding use of medium-range strike drones — while accusing him of overreaching into operational planning.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Concrete markers of Ukraine's electronic-warfare and deep-strike capability that have accumulated inside the defense ministry, independent of who holds the post.
insights.quote: He had two big achievements: disabling Starlink for the Russians and heavily expanding the use of medium-range strike drones
insights.locator: “He had two big achievements

insights.claim: Activists argue Fedorov's introduction of digital and competitive procurement systems — moving large weapons contracts away from discretionary arrangements — is what made him a target of entrenched interests.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Procurement transparency in Ukraine is politically fragile; contract-award rules can revert with personnel, changing the competitive landscape for arms suppliers.
insights.locator: Fedorov, activists have said, collided with that post-Soviet culture

insights.claim: Technology cannot substitute for soldiers in Ukraine's war: the army's manpower problem remains unresolved and Ukraine is simultaneously short of air defense while Russia continues missile and drone strikes on cities.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Caps the upside of the drone-centric thesis: interceptor and air-defense demand stays structurally high, and mobilization remains the binding constraint.
insights.quote: Technology and innovation can help Ukraine, but they cannot be substitutes for soldiers.
insights.locator: However, Russia continues to batter Ukrainian cities

insights.claim: Ukraine says it has retaken 700 square kilometers so far in 2026 and has slowed Russian advances, making the front line rather than Kyiv politics the nearer-term test of the leadership change.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: A quantified battlefield baseline against which to judge whether the command reshuffle produces measurable results.
insights.locator: Whatever Fedorov chooses, his political future

insights.claim: Fedorov built independent public standing few in Zelensky's administration possess by shipping the Diia mobile app, which made passports, driver's licenses and other government services accessible in a state previously defined by paper files, queues and small bribes.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: In post-Soviet states, delivered digital-government products now convert directly into electoral capital — a template for identifying future political risk and talent.
insights.locator: Fedorov made his name as Ukraine’s first minister

insights.claim: A source close to Zelensky said Fedorov's digital-state legacy has made him effectively untouchable because it is the one durable achievement that will outlast the current administration.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Signals that even insiders expect Fedorov to survive politically — relevant to who governs Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and digital procurement.
insights.quote: This is the only good thing that remains after we are out of power. So, I think he’s become untouchable to some extent.
insights.locator: “He made the digital passport, digital everything,”

insights.claim: Kyiv-based DEJURE Foundation director Mykhailo Zhernakov frames the conflict as being about command style rather than personalities, arguing the clash arose because too many decisions are made in one office instead of by law.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Rule-of-law reform, not personnel churn, is the variable EU accession and donor conditionality should be watching.
insights.quote: If, as a country, we had followed the law, we would not have had this conflict. But many decisions are made in one office that we all know, and that is why the conflict emerged.
insights.locator: “People recognize that Syrskyi has many achievements,”

insights.claim: A survey taken just before Syrskyi's removal found 72 percent of Ukrainians opposed Fedorov's dismissal versus 5 percent in support, with 55 percent wanting Syrskyi gone.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Quantifies how badly the presidential office misjudged public opinion — a measurable governance-quality signal for sovereign risk assessment.
insights.locator: A recent survey, conducted just before news

insights.claim: Trust in Fedorov nearly doubled from 35 percent to 65 percent while trust in Syrskyi collapsed from 39 percent to 23 percent during the crisis, meaning the firing manufactured a rival rather than removing one.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Attempted political neutralization now backfires in Ukraine's information environment; expect Zelensky's rivals to gain from confrontation with him.
insights.locator: The survey showed that trust in Fedorov nearly doubled

insights.claim: In a hypothetical Ukrainian presidential election Fedorov polls third at 13.4 percent, behind Zelensky at 22.3 percent and Valerii Zaluzhnyi at 14.9 percent — a fragmented field with no dominant successor.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: Post-war Ukrainian politics looks like a three-way scramble with low incumbent support — pricing risk for anyone assuming policy continuity after elections resume.
insights.locator: And in a hypothetical presidential election

insights.claim: Zelensky has a repeated pattern of neutralizing popular figures administratively — sending Valerii Zaluzhnyi to London as ambassador in 2024 once his ratings surpassed the president's, and appointing celebrated spy chief Kyrylo Budanov as chief of staff, a post that traditionally absorbs political blame.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: A repeatable playbook: when a Ukrainian official's polling exceeds Zelensky's, expect a lateral 'promotion' — a forecastable political event.

insights.claim: A Ukrainian government source said Fedorov has political ambition and would be ready for elections rather than accepting a lesser post, framing his choice as accept and fade, refuse and lead opposition, or be reinstated as a team player.
insights.speaker: Ani Chkhikvadze
insights.so_what: A credible opposition pole forming around a pro-technology, anti-corruption platform would change Ukraine's post-war policy trajectory.
insights.quote: He has ambition and wants to be in politics, so I would assume he will be ready for elections.
insights.locator: What does Fedorov want next?
